findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Forecast Outturn for General Fund, Housing Revenue Account (HRA) and Capital Programme
findings.headline: HRA contractor transition from sole supplier to new framework caused maintenance delivery delays
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account transitioned from a sole contractor model to a new major repairs framework in 2025-26. This transition caused delays during the procurement and assurance phase, resulting in significantly reduced maintenance activity and lower management input than budgeted. Housing repairs and maintenance were disrupted during this period.
findings.matters: Delays in housing repairs and maintenance affect tenant satisfaction, housing stock condition, and the council's ability to meet landlord obligations; also indicates potential contractor capacity or coordination risks
findings.figures: Management Fee underspend £756k; Repairs and Maintenance underspend £591k; £566k maintenance resources diverted to capital programme support
findings.quote: Delays in the mobilisation of the new major works arrangements, following the decision to transition away from a sole contractor model. Reduced activity during the procurement and assurance phase resulted in lower management input than originally profiled

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Forecast Outturn for General Fund, Housing Revenue Account (HRA) and Capital Programme
findings.headline: PSDS3 capital schemes abandoned or paused due to cost escalation and grant compliance challenges
findings.detail: Two PSDS3 schemes were abandoned or suspended in 2025-26 due to cost escalation. Hucknall Leisure Centre PSDS3 was cancelled following cost escalation and discovery that the site is Trust land, with ongoing uncertainty about grant position with Salix. Urban Road Offices PSDS3 was not progressed due to 'significant cost escalation, affordability concerns and challenges in meeting long-term grant monitoring requirements'. The council incurred design and procurement costs before abandoning both schemes.
findings.matters: Cost escalation forcing scheme cancellation indicates cost control challenges and risks loss of government grants, both material concerns for lenders assessing financial management
findings.figures: Hucknall Leisure Centre PSDS3: £1,322k underspend (near-total non-delivery); Urban Road: £115k expended before abandonment
findings.quote: The PSDS3 scheme at Hucknall Leisure Centre was effectively cancelled in 2025-26 following cost escalation and legal advice confirming the site is Trust land

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Forecast Outturn for General Fund, Housing Revenue Account (HRA) and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Procurement and governance breaches identified on ADMC capital project requiring suspension and rephasing
findings.detail: The ADMC phase was suspended in 2025-26 following identification of procurement and governance breaches. Construction expenditure was reprofiled and the completion timeline was revised. The council states no loss of funding occurred and the scheme recommenced in May 2026, but the breaches identified raise questions about the strength of capital programme controls.
findings.matters: Procurement and governance failures directly undermine confidence in the council's ability to manage capital projects and public money, matters that lenders and finance directors cannot overlook
findings.figures: £756k underspend on Management Fee element in HRA capital budget due to project suspension
findings.quote: suspension of the ADMC phase following identification of procurement and governance breaches, resulting in reprofiling of construction spend and a revised completion timeline

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Quarter 1 - Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Substantial capital programme slippage from prior year indicates ongoing delivery challenges
findings.detail: The council is carrying forward £13.7m of unspent General Fund capital and £2.4m of HRA capital from 2025/26 into 2026/27. New major works contracts are being finalised with expected further slippage into 2027/28 affecting delivery performance across the portfolio.
findings.matters: Persistent slippage suggests the council struggles with capital delivery and project execution, which affects its ability to deliver strategic objectives and may signal capacity or governance issues.
findings.figures: General Fund slippage £13.723m; HRA slippage £2.474m; additional expected slippage into 2027/28
findings.quote: With the time remaining in the financial year, it is likely that there will be some slippage of the program into 2027/28. Hardwick Lane development on track to be under budget, with other schemes likely to have slippage into 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Quarter 1 - Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Unexpected £170k increase in agency costs for vacant positions and Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The council is incurring additional agency costs of £170k to cover vacant positions and to manage anticipated increases from Local Government Reorganisation. The report notes these costs are expected to be funded from vacant positions and reserves.
findings.matters: Growing unplanned expenditure, funded from reserves, indicates the council is under financial pressure and draining reserves to cover operational shortfalls.
findings.figures: £170k additional agency costs
findings.quote: A movement of £170k for additional agency costs, associated with covering of vacant positions and in relation to the anticipated increase in costs associated with the Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Quarter 1 - Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Major savings plan failing: £200k of £330k planned savings will not be achieved
findings.detail: The council planned £330k of savings and efficiencies for 2026/27, but only £130k (39%) are forecast to be delivered. Most significantly, the £200k 'Review of contract, specifically agency model' saving will not be achieved due to ongoing land issues. This represents a 60% shortfall in the largest single saving.
findings.matters: Persistent failure to deliver planned savings is a credit concern for lenders, indicating either optimistic planning or underlying operational challenges preventing execution.
findings.figures: £130k achieved of £330k planned (39%); £200k single saving will not be achieved
findings.quote: The position outlined above shows £130k of the £330k savings are forecast to be achieved.   The item in red: Review of contract, specifically agency model will not be achieved due to ongoing land issues.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Treasury Management - 4th Quarter.
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing costs have risen sharply, with 10-year gilt yields increasing to approximately 5% by March 2026 from 4.2% in February
findings.detail: Financial market conditions deteriorated during late 2025/26. Long-term gilt yields (which benchmark council external borrowing costs) increased materially from 4.2% in February to approximately 5% by March 2026. The paper attributes this to 'higher inflation expectations, a reassessment of the future path of interest rates, and increased global uncertainty', particularly Middle East tensions impacting energy prices. Earlier expectations of rate reductions reversed.
findings.matters: As Ashfield's reserves deplete (£12m/year currently) and faces £85.6m capital spending in 2026/27, it will likely need to access external borrowing. It will do so in a materially higher rate environment, directly increasing debt servicing costs and reducing affordability of capital projects.
findings.figures: 10-year gilt yields: 4.2% (February 2026) to approximately 5% (March 2026)
findings.quote: Ten-year gilt yields increased from around 4.2% in February to approximately 5% by March 2026. This movement represents a material increase in borrowing costs and has direct implications for both government and local authority financing.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Treasury Management - 4th Quarter.
findings.headline: Investment balances declined by £12.4m to £39.1m, reflecting accelerating depletion of internal cash reserves used to fund capital
findings.detail: The council's investment holdings fell from £51.5m to £39.1m during 2025/26, with this decline reflecting use of cash reserves to finance capital activity. The council maintains 'a continued strategy of internal borrowing', using cash rather than external debt. At a depletion rate of £12.4m per year, the remaining reserves would be exhausted in approximately three years, forcing reliance on external borrowing.
findings.matters: Cash reserves are finite and provide a buffer against unexpected costs. As they deplete, the council will be forced to rely on external borrowing sooner than planned, and at current interest rates this is more expensive. The sustainability of this reserves-based financing strategy is limited.
findings.figures: Investment balances: £51.5m (31 Mar 2025) to £39.1m (31 Mar 2026); £12.4m decline (24% reduction)
findings.quote: Investment balances have reduced from £51.5m to £39.1m, reflecting the use of cash reserves to finance capital activity.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Treasury Management - 4th Quarter.
findings.headline: General Fund financing cost ratio rising from 11.6% to 12.9% by 2027/28, driven by reduced government funding and increased debt repayment obligations
findings.detail: The proportion of General Fund net revenue consumed by capital financing costs is forecast to rise from 11.60% in 2025/26 to 12.93% in 2027/28. The council attributes this to reduced government funding and increased MRP charges arising from the capital programme. This leaves less revenue available for service delivery and other expenditure, reducing financial flexibility and headroom for unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: A rising financing cost ratio indicates shrinking financial headroom. With more of the council's core income (council tax and government grants) committed to debt servicing, there is less flexibility to absorb financial shocks or invest in services without additional borrowing.
findings.quote: The Ratio for the General Fund increases from 2026/27 as a result of reduced Government funding and increased MRP charges due to Capital Programme Developments.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Treasury Management - 4th Quarter.
findings.headline: General Fund capital spending missed forecast by 63%, raising questions about project delivery capability and forecast credibility for the 2026/27 expansion
findings.detail: General Fund capital expenditure was only £14.0m in 2025/26 against a forecast of £37.5m, representing a £23.5m shortfall and re-profiling of schemes. The paper acknowledges 'delays in the delivery of major schemes'. HRA spending offset part of this underspend by exceeding forecast (£20.2m actual vs £11.6m estimate), but the General Fund variance is material and raises whether the significantly more ambitious 2026/27 forecast of £60.6m can be delivered.
findings.matters: Material forecast misses indicate either constrained delivery capacity or planning uncertainty. For a lender, this raises concerns about whether the council can execute an £85.6m programme (2.5x what General Fund actually spent in 2025/26) and whether capital forecasts are reliable.
findings.figures: General Fund 2025/26: £37.5m forecast, £14.0m actual (63% underspend)
findings.quote: Total capital expenditure in 2025/26 was £34.2m, significantly below the original estimate of £49.1m, indicating slippage and re-profiling within the capital programme. This variance is primarily attributable to the General Fund, where outturn reduced to £14.0m against an estimate of £37.5m, suggesting delays in the delivery of major schemes.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Treasury Management - 4th Quarter.
findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast to surge to £85.6m in 2026/27, more than double 2025/26 actual, requiring substantial additional financing
findings.detail: The council's capital programme shows a step change from £34.2m in 2025/26 to a planned £85.6m in 2026/27, driven mainly by General Fund schemes (£60.6m). The paper describes this as the 'commencement or acceleration of major regeneration and capital schemes' including 'town centre regeneration, housing growth, and economic development'. This expansion will require substantial financing through a mix of internal resources and external borrowing, placing upward pressure on the Capital Financing Requirement.
findings.matters: The scale of this expansion signals a major financing event ahead. The council will likely need to increase external borrowing and/or further deplete its cash reserves, directly affecting debt serviceability and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 2025/26 actual £34.2m; 2026/27 forecast £85.6m (150% increase); General Fund component £60.6m
findings.quote: Looking forward, there is a substantial step change in 2026/27, with total capital expenditure projected to rise to £85.6m, driven predominantly by the General Fund (£60.6m). This step change represents the delivery phase of major General Fund schemes alongside continued HRA investment and will require a substantial increase in financing through a mix of internal resources and, where necessary, external borrowing.

findings.paper_title: AGS 2025-26 June 2026 v4 For Audit Committee
findings.headline: General Reserve level unconfirmed at year-end, creating uncertainty over liquidity buffer
findings.detail: The statement notes that the council's General Reserve as at 31 March 2026 was marked as TBC (to be confirmed), only noting it was above the minimum required balance. The actual reserve position was not disclosed in this governance statement, preventing assessment of the council's liquidity cushion.
findings.matters: Reserves are the primary buffer against funding shocks and unexpected costs. A council unwilling or unable to disclose reserve levels in its governance statement raises questions about reserve adequacy and financial stability.
findings.figures: General Reserve at 31st March 2026 was TBC; TBC above minimum required balance
findings.quote: The Council's General Reserve at 31st March 2026 was TBC; TBC above the minimum required balance as set out in the Council's Constitution.

findings.paper_title: AGS 2025-26 June 2026 v4 For Audit Committee
findings.headline: Sole trustee of charitable trust land with historic breach of charitable purposes requiring rectification
findings.detail: The council identified itself as sole trustee of charitable trust land (including green spaces) conveyed to the council for public pleasure or recreation. Some areas have been built on in breach of the charitable purposes, and the council is committed to regulating these historic charity land issues. This is noted as an ongoing improvement action.
findings.matters: As sole trustee of charitable land built on in breach of trust, the council faces potential legal liability and remediation costs. This is a contingent liability not quantified in the statement.
findings.figures: Number and value of affected land areas not disclosed
findings.quote: Some areas of charitable trust land have been identified as having been built on in breach of the charitable purposes, and the Council is committed to regulating these historic charity land issues.

findings.paper_title: AGS 2025-26 June 2026 v4 For Audit Committee
findings.headline: Staff turnover and interim leadership in finance function during critical system implementation
findings.detail: An Interim Corporate Resources Director was appointed in November 2025 (described as CIPFA qualified with 35 years experience), with recruitment underway for a permanent Executive Director, Corporate Resources role during 26/27. This recruitment gap occurred during critical implementation of the new financial system, which the statement links to delays and control failures.
findings.matters: Staff turnover and reliance on interim leadership in the finance function weakens control during a critical implementation period. It creates continuity risk and may explain some of the governance and accounts delays.
findings.figures: Interim CRD appointed November 2025; permanent role to be recruited in 26/27
findings.quote: The Interim CRD (through 25/26) was appointed in November 2025 and is a CIPFA qualified accountant with over 35 years post-qualification experience across both the private and public sector, undertaking many similar roles.

findings.paper_title: AGS 2025-26 June 2026 v4 For Audit Committee
findings.headline: Financial sustainability at risk with one-year settlement and uncertainty over future central government funding
findings.detail: The council received another one-year financial settlement with significant uncertainty about central government funding from 2026/27, linked to Local Government Finance Reform. The MTFS was described as painting a worst-case scenario without a detailed programme to close the funding gap at the time the budget was set. The council is implementing zero-based budgeting to address the challenge.
findings.matters: One-year settlements and unresolved funding gaps force reliance on reserves and make multi-year financial planning impossible. This constrains the council's ability to invest or service additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Specific funding gap figures not disclosed in this statement
findings.quote: Following another one-year Financial Settlement, there remains significant uncertainty about the level of Central Government funding from 2026/27, linked to the implementation of Local Government Finance Reform.

findings.paper_title: AGS 2025-26 June 2026 v4 For Audit Committee
findings.headline: Corporate Assurance Assessment score dropped significantly due to governance issues
findings.detail: The council's self-assessed Corporate Assurance Assessment score of 86% is described as lower than previous years, explicitly attributed to the governance issues detailed in the statement (Section 5A report, financial system implementation, project governance failures).
findings.matters: A declining assurance score signals deterioration in the control environment and is consistent with the Limited Assurance audit opinion; it suggests multiple governance weaknesses, not isolated incidents.
findings.figures: 86% score recorded; previous years scored higher
findings.quote: A score of 86% was recorded. This is a lower score than previous years largely due to governance issues described below.

findings.paper_title: AGS 2025-26 June 2026 v4 For Audit Committee
findings.headline: New financial system implementation delayed, causing delayed statutory accounts production and ongoing issues
findings.detail: The new core financial ledger went live during 2024 but implementation faced significant delays, causing the 2024/25 statutory accounts to be delayed until January 2026. Further phases of implementation are ongoing and due to complete in 26/27. The statement notes this arose from staffing pressures and turnover in key roles, and IT system audits are still underway.
findings.matters: Failures to implement financial systems on time indicate weak project governance and resourcing. Delayed accounts prevent timely financial decision-making, and ongoing implementation work suggests controls remain unstable.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Council has been implementing a new financial ledger that went live in 2024. The full implementation has faced delays, and consequently, the statutory accounts production was delayed.

findings.paper_title: AGS 2025-26 June 2026 v4 For Audit Committee
findings.headline: External Audit disclaimed opinion on 2024/25 financial statements and unable to conclude on value for money
findings.detail: External Audit issued a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements, and a subsequent VFM update report in April 2026 confirmed they were unable to conclude on VFM arrangements due to the significant governance issue identified by the Section 5A report. The 2024/25 Statement of Accounts was published in January 2026, delayed from normal deadlines.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means External Audit could not provide reasonable assurance over the accuracy of the financial statements. This is the most serious audit outcome and prevents any reliance on published accounts for assessing financial position.
findings.figures: 2024/25 accounts published in January 2026 (delayed); 2025/26 accounts due by 30 June 2026
findings.quote: The Council received a disclaimed opinion for 2024/25 financial statements from its External Audit partners.

findings.paper_title: AGS 2025-26 June 2026 v4 For Audit Committee
findings.headline: Internal audit gave only Limited Assurance due to governance and financial system concerns
findings.detail: CMAP concluded that only Limited Assurance can be given on the adequacy and effectiveness of the Council's governance, risk management and control framework. The opinion specifically cited significant concerns over governance of major projects and implementation and operation of the Council's financial system, with a note that actions taken are not yet sufficiently advanced to confirm effectiveness.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance is a significant downgrade from typical unqualified opinions and signals that internal controls are materially deficient in managing major risks.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Only Limited Assurance can be given on the adequacy and effectiveness of the Council's framework of governance, risk management and control due to significant concerns over the governance of major projects and the implementation and operation of the Council's financial system.

findings.paper_title: AGS 2025-26 June 2026 v4 For Audit Committee
findings.headline: Monitoring Officer issued formal Section 5A report over breach of law on major capital project
findings.detail: In March 2026, the Monitoring Officer published a Section 5A report regarding the Automated Distribution and Manufacturing Centre project, detailing governance issues and non-compliance with Contract Procedure Rules and Financial Regulations. The council has since established a Corporate Project Assurance Board to oversee governance, but the issues suggest control failures on a significant capital scheme.
findings.matters: Breach of law on capital projects signals weak project governance and financial controls, both material to a lender's assessment of the council's ability to manage major schemes and protect public resources.
findings.figures: Regeneration funding co-funding of over £132m mentioned; specific project value not disclosed
findings.quote: On 31 March 2026, the Monitoring Officer published a Section 5A Local Government and Housing Act 1989 report (the Act) (S5A Report) in relation to contractual and procurement issues associated with the Automated Distribution and Manufacturing Centre project. The issues involved some non-compliance with the Council's Contract Procedure Rules and Financial Regulations in relation to the project.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management - 4th Quarter.
findings.headline: General Fund financing costs rising to 12.93% of net revenue stream by 2027/28, up from 11.60% in 2025/26
findings.detail: The report attributes this increase to reduced government funding and increased MRP charges from capital programme developments. This means more of the council's core revenue (council tax and grants) is committed to debt servicing, reducing discretionary flexibility in the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Rising financing cost ratios as a proportion of revenue stream are a key affordability indicator; they show reduced capacity to absorb spending pressures or invest in services, and constrain the council's financial flexibility.
findings.quote: The Ratio for the General Fund increases from 2026/27 as a result of reduced Government funding and increased MRP charges due to Capital Programme Developments.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management - 4th Quarter.
findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure to increase from £14.0m in 2025/26 to £60.6m in 2026/27, a 333% step change
findings.detail: The report projects a substantial expansion of capital activity from 2026/27, driven by major regeneration and housing growth schemes. This will significantly increase the authority's underlying borrowing need and capital financing requirement, requiring careful treasury planning and greater reliance on internal and external borrowing.
findings.matters: A major capital acceleration of this scale determines the council's debt trajectory, cash flow requirements, and future debt servicing capacity, and is directly material to lending decisions.
findings.figures: 2025/26 actual £14.0m → 2026/27 estimate £60.6m; borrowing requirement rising from £5.323m to £30.595m
findings.quote: Looking forward, there is a substantial step change in 2026/27, with total capital expenditure projected to rise to £85.6m, driven predominantly by the General Fund (£60.6m). This indicates the commencement or acceleration of major regeneration and capital schemes, likely aligned to previously approved Cabinet programmes and strategic priorities such as town centre regeneration, housing growth, and economic development.

findings.paper_title: ADC Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Plan delivery slipped: Internal audit completed only 80% of planned work against 90% target
findings.detail: Internal Audit achieved 80% of its planned audit work in 2025-26, against a performance target of 90%. The report notes this reflects 'unforeseen priorities that divert resources from the original plan, resource constraints, changes in business environment, access and cooperation delays and audit scope requiring expansion'.
findings.matters: Failure to complete planned audit work means the council did not get the level of independent assurance it expected. Combined with multiple significant issues emerging (major project failures, system implementation problems), this suggests audit resource may be insufficient for the risk environment.
findings.figures: 80% audit plan delivered (target 90%)
findings.quote: In 2025-26, we achieved 80% of the plan.

findings.paper_title: ADC Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council involved in county-wide local government reorganisation proposals introducing substantial governance risks
findings.detail: The council is actively involved in county-wide proposals for local government reorganisation (LGR). The audit identifies this as 'a developing governance challenge, that introduces substantial governance risks' including organisational change, future governance structures, financial resilience, partnership governance, programme management, and workforce capacity.
findings.matters: LGR creates significant uncertainty and execution risk. During reorganisation, governance often becomes diffuse, decision-making slows, and focus fragments. Combined with existing control weaknesses, this creates a window where issues could worsen or go unmanaged.
findings.figures: County-wide LGR proposals identified as introducing substantial governance risks across multiple areas
findings.quote: The Council has been actively involved in county-wide proposals for local government reorganisation (LGR). This is a developing governance challenge, that introduces substantial governance risks around: Organisational change. Future governance structures. Financial resilience. Partnership governance. Programme management. Workforce capacity.

findings.paper_title: ADC Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit Committee effectiveness under scrutiny due to lack of member challenge and understanding of its role
findings.detail: The audit report notes that 'The overall performance of the Audit Committee is under scrutiny due to the ongoing lack of challenge and understanding from Members in respect of its role and responsibilities.' In response, the council created an Audit Committee Improvement Plan. Revised membership and chairmanship, plus training, have already taken place.
findings.matters: An Audit Committee without effective challenge is a governance control failure. If elected members do not understand or challenge audit findings, internal control weaknesses are less likely to be escalated and remedied. This is a secondary risk amplifier.
findings.figures: Audit Committee effectiveness under scrutiny; Improvement Plan created; revised membership and training delivered
findings.quote: The effectiveness of the Audit Committee was also noted as an area of concern. The overall performance of the Audit Committee is under scrutiny due to the ongoing lack of challenge and understanding from Members in respect of its role and responsibilities.

findings.paper_title: ADC Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Corporate Resources Director and Section 151 Officer departed October 2025; interim replacement in post since November 2025 after unsuccessful permanent recruitment
findings.detail: The Council's S151 Officer (chief finance officer) and Corporate Resources Director left in October 2025. Interim arrangements were put in place, and a suitably qualified interim post-holder took up the role in November 2025. A subsequent recruitment exercise to appoint someone permanently was unsuccessful, and the current interim post-holder remains in post.
findings.matters: The S151 Officer is the key financial leadership role and statutory responsibility holder. Loss of permanent, experienced finance leadership combined with failed recruitment to replace them creates continuity and expertise risk. An interim CFO for an extended period signals difficulty attracting permanent talent.
findings.figures: Departure October 2025; interim since November 2025; permanent recruitment unsuccessful
findings.quote: Following the departure of the Corporate Resources Director and S151 Officer in October 2025, interim arrangements were put in place to ensure key financial functions were supported. A suitably qualified and experienced interim Corporate Resources Director and Section S151 Officer has been in place since November 2025. Following an unsuccessful recruitment exercise to recruit to the post permanently, the current interim post holder remains in post.

findings.paper_title: ADC Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: External auditor Forvis Mazars found significant weaknesses in financial sustainability and governance; 2024-25 accounts not yet concluded due to value for money concern
findings.detail: The external auditor (Forvis Mazars) noted significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements for both financial sustainability and governance. Work on the 2024-25 Accounts had not concluded as of the Audit Committee meeting (25 June 2026) due to a value for money concern identified by the auditor.
findings.matters: External audit findings of significant weakness, combined with unresolved value for money concerns holding up accounts sign-off, signal material control or reporting issues. Delayed account closure indicates auditor concerns remain unresolved.
findings.figures: Forvis Mazars identified significant weaknesses in financial sustainability and governance; 2024-25 accounts not concluded as of 25 June 2026 meeting
findings.quote: Forvis Mazars, the Council's external auditor has noted significant weaknesses in its assessment of the Council's arrangements for both financial sustainability and governance. Forvis Mazars reported to the March Audit Committee that work has not yet concluded on the 2024-25 Accounts due to a value for money concern.

findings.paper_title: ADC Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Major project governance failures across multiple schemes; Monitoring Officer issued formal Section 5A report on ADMC project for governance and procurement breaches
findings.detail: The council has systemic governance weaknesses across major projects. For the Automated Distribution and Manufacturing Centre (ADMC) project, the Monitoring Officer formally reported breaches of established governance and procurement processes to all Members on 31 March 2026 under Section 5A of the Local Government and Housing Act 1989. An independent review identified 'learning points'. Risks identified include 'loss of funding, failure to deliver economic benefits, legal challenge and reputational damage'.
findings.matters: A Monitoring Officer Section 5A report is a formal escalation indicating potential illegality or maladministration. Combined with risks of lost funding and legal challenge, this signals potential liability and loss of external grant income. It also indicates governance failure at senior level.
findings.figures: Section 5A report issued 31 March 2026; risks include loss of funding, failure to deliver economic benefits, legal challenge and reputational damage
findings.quote: On 31 March 2026, the Monitoring Officer sent a section 5A Local Government and Housing Act 1989 report to all Members in relation to the ADMC project. The report outlined that the Council's established governance and procurement processes had not been followed in relation to some aspects of the ADMC Project.

findings.paper_title: ADC Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme received No Assurance rating with overspends in excess of £2m and failure to follow Contract Procedure Rules
findings.detail: Internal Audit reviewed the scheme at the Executive Director's request after potential governance issues were identified. The audit identified three low, seven moderate, and two significant risk issues. Findings include failure to follow Contract Procedure Rules, payments to contractors without formal contracts, poor risk management, weak contractor management, and accounting errors. The scheme was given a No Assurance rating (the lowest).
findings.matters: A major project overrun of £2m+ combined with governance failures and No Assurance rating shows the council struggles to manage large capital schemes. This risks project failure, value loss, and contractual disputes. It also signals reputational damage and potential clawback of external funding.
findings.figures: Overspends in excess of £2m; No Assurance rating (immediate action required); two significant risk, seven moderate risk, three low risk issues identified
findings.quote: The Executive Director – Governance requested that Internal Audit review this scheme as potential governance issues had been identified by the Council and overspends in excess of £2m. The audit identified three low risk, seven moderate risk and two significant risk issues and the subject area was given 'No Assurance'.

findings.paper_title: ADC Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Finance system implementation causing late payments, inability to reconcile accounts, and misstated budget monitoring
findings.detail: Ashfield's implementation of Technology One has created 'substantial operational challenges' including misaligned authorisation processes, difficulties with budget monitoring, late invoice payments, and inability to complete reconciliations. The Council Tax account was not fully reconciled to the General Ledger since July 2024. Related audit reviews found weaknesses in access controls, stale user accounts, and inappropriate permissions within the finance system.
findings.matters: A finance system that cannot reconcile accounts or enforce controls undermines financial reporting reliability and creates operational risk. If the council cannot track its own money correctly, lenders cannot trust its financial position. Late payments also signal cash-flow pressure.
findings.figures: Council Tax account not reconciled since July 2024; Finance System – Access Management & Systems Administration audit rated Limited Assurance with four moderate risk recommendations
findings.quote: The initial system migration created substantial operational challenges including the misaligned authorisation processes, difficulties with budget monitoring, late invoice payments and an inability to complete key reconciliations.

findings.paper_title: ADC Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: £18m cumulative funding gap in 2026-27 and 2027-28 with no robust plan to close it
findings.detail: The external auditor Forvis Mazars identified a £18m funding gap in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy alongside the 2025-26 budget approval. The report notes the council has 'no robust plan on how to close this gap' and that Mazars reported significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements for financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A £18m gap with no identified solution is material to lenders. It shows the council faces severe budget pressure with unclear mitigation, raising questions about repayment capacity and financial resilience over two years.
findings.figures: £18m cumulative funding gap in 2026-27 and 2027-28
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy that was approved alongside the 2025-26 budget highlighted a cumulative potential funding gap of £18m in 2026-27 and 2027-28 with no robust plan on how to close this gap.

findings.paper_title: ADC Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Limited Assurance given on governance and control due to significant weaknesses in major project governance and financial system implementation
findings.detail: The Chief Audit Executive's conclusion is Limited Assurance (one of four possible ratings), the second-lowest. This reflects serious concerns about how the council governs major projects and operates its finance system. The audit notes that whilst management has committed to remedial action, these actions are not yet sufficiently advanced to show they work.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance on governance and control is a red flag for lenders. It signals control breakdowns, audit findings of high-risk or systemic issues, and material weaknesses in how the council manages money and major commitments.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance (second-lowest of four ratings)
findings.quote: Only Limited Assurance can be given on the adequacy and effectiveness of the Council's framework of governance, risk management and control due to significant concerns over the governance of major projects and the implementation and operation of the Council's financial system.

findings.paper_title: ADC 2024-25 Audit Opinion Update June 2026
findings.headline: 2024/25 audit opinion delayed pending completion of value-for-money investigation into governance failures
findings.detail: The 2024/25 audit opinion on the financial statements has still not been issued as of June 2026, three months into the new financial year. The auditor is completing additional value-for-money work and awaiting further responses from the council and MHCLG before finalisation.
findings.matters: A delayed audit opinion three months into the new year, particularly driven by governance failures in a major capital project, signals elevated audit risk and may affect the council's borrowing capacity or terms.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: At the 19 March Audit Committee meeting, we provided a verbal update confirming that the 2024/25 opinion on the Council's financial statements has not yet been issued due to the additional value-for-money work required.

findings.paper_title: ADC 2024-25 Audit Opinion Update June 2026
findings.headline: Material errors identified in 2024/25 financial statements requiring investigation
findings.detail: The auditor has been alerted to material errors in the 2024/25 financial statements which must be investigated before the audit opinion is finalised. The nature and quantum of these errors are not disclosed in this document.
findings.matters: Material errors in the financial statements would affect the reliability of the council's financial position that lenders and finance directors depend on.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: We have also been alerted to the possibility of material errors in the 2024/25 financial statements, which need to be investigated prior to completion.

findings.paper_title: ADC 2024-25 Audit Opinion Update June 2026
findings.headline: ADMC project ongoing and requires updated business case and additional capital funding
findings.detail: The council must resolve how to proceed with the ADMC and needs to receive and approve an updated business case and secure additional capital funding beyond the original £19m allocation. This follows the governance failures and cost escalations already identified.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the total capital commitment, whether additional funding can be sourced, and whether the council's governance weaknesses put that funding at risk.
findings.figures: £19m already allocated
findings.quote: As the project is ongoing, the Council also needs to receive and approve an updated business case and agree additional capital funding for the ADMC and associated projects.

findings.paper_title: ADC 2024-25 Audit Opinion Update June 2026
findings.headline: Monitoring Officer's Section 5A report identifies systemic governance failures on £19m ADMC capital project
findings.detail: The Monitoring Officer issued a formal Section 5A report on 31 March 2026 identifying that the council failed to comply with its own Contract Procedure Rules and Financial Regulations. The council entered into works and made payments without signed contracts in place, received inadequate procurement advice, and failed to monitor escalating project costs. The failures occurred over a prolonged period and reflect deficiencies in risk assessment and compliance.
findings.matters: The auditor concludes this represents evidence of significant weaknesses in the Council's governance arrangements that expose it to significant risk of further unlawful decision making, potential financial loss, and legal challenge.
findings.figures: £19m allocated by MHCLG under Towns' Fund initiative
findings.quote: The Council did not comply with its own Contract Procedure Rules and Financial Regulations in the delivery of the ADMC project, with numerous failings including inadequate procurement advice, insufficient evidence to demonstrate compliance with the Public Contracts Regulations 2025, works proceeding without a contract in place, payments made to suppliers without a contract and inadequate arrangements for monitoring and controlling escalating project costs.

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Approval
findings.headline: Property team has acknowledged resource and expertise shortfall to execute asset disposal program
findings.detail: The council states that delivering the rationalization will require additional staff and external advisors beyond current property team capacity.
findings.matters: Understaffed execution teams delay disposal timelines and risk suboptimal sales; if the council cannot execute its own strategy, debt repayment may slip.
findings.figures: Staffing gap requiring additional resources and external advisors
findings.quote: Lack of resources and expertise in the property team will result in additional resource required to deliver rationalisation team with support from external advisors where required.

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Approval
findings.headline: Council has prohibited all new out-of-district acquisitions, reversing prior investment strategy
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly rules out any future acquisitions outside the district. This is a hard stop on the approach that built the now-declining portfolio.
findings.matters: The ban acknowledges that prior out-of-district acquisitions failed; a lender would want assurance that decision-making governance has improved and this pattern will not repeat.
findings.figures: Policy change to zero future out-of-district acquisitions
findings.quote: Confirmation that no new out-of-district investments will be made.

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Approval
findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset disposals must first repay legacy borrowing (Minimal Revenue Provision), not support reinvestment
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly directs all disposal proceeds to offset MRP liabilities before any can be reinvested locally. This prioritization signals that the council's debt burden from these acquisitions is substantial enough to warrant prioritizing repayment.
findings.matters: The size of MRP obligations created by these investments is material; a lender would want to know the quantum of legacy debt and the timeline for repayment through asset sales.
findings.figures: Capital receipts → Minimal Revenue Provision reduction → surplus to in-district reinvestment
findings.quote: Direct that capital receipts from any disposals be applied first to offset associated borrowing (reducing Minimal Revenue Provision (MRP) liabilities), with any surplus considered for reinvestment in-district priorities.

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Approval
findings.headline: External property portfolio has experienced consistent value decline across most assets as of March 2026
findings.detail: The council's March 2026 valuation confirms downward movement in capital values across the majority of the out-of-district portfolio. This decline prompted the shift from passive holding to active rationalization, indicating these commercial investments have underperformed expectations.
findings.matters: Asset value deterioration directly affects balance sheet strength and reduces the council's financial flexibility; a lender needs to understand the scale and speed of the decline and what remains.
findings.figures: External portfolio valuation results 31 March 2026; consistent downward movement across majority of assets
findings.quote: recent external portfolio valuation results (31 March 2026) which show a net downward movement in capital values across the majority of assets

findings.paper_title: ADC Value for Money Update March 26 - to issue
findings.headline: Audit Committee remains ineffective in challenge and oversight, a weakness identified in July 2023 that persists through September 2025
findings.detail: Internal Audit in July 2023 and Corporate Peer Challenge 2023/24 both identified improvement needs in Audit Committee effectiveness. Despite these recommendations, auditor observations through September 2025 show continuing poor levels of challenge from Audit Committee members and lack of effectiveness.
findings.matters: An ineffective Audit Committee means weak second-line oversight of management and internal controls. For lenders, this suggests the council's internal governance system is not functioning, reducing confidence in the control environment.
findings.figures: Weakness identified July 2023; re-identified 2023/24; persisting through September 2025 (over two years)
findings.quote: Our meetings with officers and our attendance at Audit Committee meetings since then and up to and including September 2025 showed continuing poor levels of challenge from the Audit Committee, resulting in a lack of effectiveness.

findings.paper_title: ADC Value for Money Update March 26 - to issue
findings.headline: 2024/25 financial outturn not reported until 23 December 2025, nine months after year-end, leaving council without reliable budget position
findings.detail: The new financial ledger difficulties prevented budget monitoring throughout 2024/25. The outturn was not reported until late December 2025, well after normal closedown. Without timely outturn data and clear reporting of actual expenditure, the council cannot take effective action on financial performance or set the 2026/27 budget with confidence.
findings.matters: Delayed financial reporting prevents the council from managing in-year performance, identifying cost pressures early, or responding to overspends. For lenders, this suggests weak financial control and inability to make timely corrective decisions.
findings.figures: Outturn reported 23 December 2025 (nine months after 31 March 2025 year-end)
findings.quote: The Council went live on a new financial ledger in August 2024, which created difficulties in budget monitoring and did not report its 2024/25 financial outturn position until 23 December 2025. Without a 2024/25 outturn and clearer reporting of actual expenditure incurred to date, the Council is unable to take effective action on financial performance

findings.paper_title: ADC Value for Money Update March 26 - to issue
findings.headline: New financial ledger implemented August 2024 without governance arrangements; data migration assurance still incomplete as of December 2025
findings.detail: Despite being flagged as high-risk on the Corporate Risk Register, the Council did not establish governance arrangements for the ledger implementation. Assurance over data transfer between old and new systems had not been performed nine months later, preventing production of 2024/25 financial statements and outturn. The implementation also led to use of credit cards to pay suppliers.
findings.matters: Without validated financial data, the council cannot accurately track expenditure, identify overspends in-year, or set reliable budgets. This undermines financial management capability and creates audit risk. For lenders, it suggests weak operational controls over a critical system.
findings.figures: Ledger went live August 2024; assurance not completed by December 2025 (4+ months overdue)
findings.quote: A new financial ledger went live in August 2024 and despite being a high-risk item on the Corporate Risk Register, the Council did not provide evidence of governance arrangements to implementation. As at December 2025, assurance over data transfer between the old and new systems had not been performed and led to an inability to produce 2024/25 financial statements

findings.paper_title: ADC Value for Money Update March 26 - to issue
findings.headline: Auditors issued disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 financial statements due to insufficient audit evidence
findings.detail: The external auditors were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to form an opinion on the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025. The deadline pressure from the 27 February 2026 backstop date meant not all necessary audit procedures could be completed.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means no external verification that the council's financial statements are accurate or reliable. For lenders, this creates opacity around the council's true financial position and suggests material misstatements may be undetected.
findings.figures: Backstop date for publication: 27 February 2026; audit incomplete as of March 2026
findings.quote: Because of the significance of the matter described in the Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion section of our report, we have not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an audit opinion on these financial statements.

findings.paper_title: ADC Value for Money Update March 26 - to issue
findings.headline: Estimated £18m cumulative funding gap in 2026/27 and 2027/28 with no credible plan to address it
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget was approved with £4.2m use of reserves and no Council Tax increase. The Medium-Term Financial Strategy identified an unmitigated £18m gap across 2026/27 and 2027/28, which would significantly deplete useable revenue reserves if realised. The Council made only a £0.6m savings plan for 2025/26 and no plan to close the larger gap.
findings.matters: This gap, if realised, would substantially erode the council's reserves and threaten financial sustainability. For lenders, it indicates the council is not adequately planning for known budget pressures and may face reserve depletion within two years.
findings.figures: £18m cumulative funding gap 2026/27–2027/28; £4.2m reserve use in 2025/26; £0.6m savings plan for 2025/26
findings.quote: The 2025/26 MTFS included an estimated and unmitigated cumulative funding gap of £18m in 2026/27 and 2027/28, which, if realised, would have a significant impact on the Council's useable revenue reserves. Other than a £0.6m savings plan for 2025/26, the Council made no plan to close that gap.

findings.paper_title: ADC Value for Money Update March 26 - to issue
findings.headline: £5m of works undertaken without signed contracts on the £19m Automated Distribution and Manufacturing Centre Towns Fund project
findings.detail: The Chief Executive suspended all works on 9 January 2026 after the Monitoring Officer raised concerns about contract and procurement failures. The audit identifies systemic failures including failure to enter into contracts before work commenced, payment of suppliers without contracts, inadequate procurement advice, and failure to manage project costs against budget. A Section 5A report was formally issued on 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: This represents unlawful decision-making that exposes the council to significant financial loss, legal challenge, potential loss of the entire £19m Towns Fund allocation, and non-compliance with statutory duties. For lenders, it demonstrates serious deficiencies in project management controls and decision-making governance.
findings.figures: £19m Towns Fund allocation; £5m of works without contracts; £10m additional match funding from partners
findings.quote: The evidence demonstrates systemic weaknesses in governance, including failure to follow the Council's Contract Procedure Rules, failure to obtain required procurement advice, and the undertaking and payment of £5m of works without signed contracts—all of which expose the Council to significant risks of unlawful decision making, financial loss, legal challenge, and non-compliance with statutory duties.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Right to Buy receipts retained for affordable housing must be spent within a 5-year window or returned to government with interest
findings.detail: New 2024-25 arrangements require the council to recycle RTB receipts into affordable housing within 5 years. The council notes: 'If future actual expenditure matches the budgeted expenditure in the capital programme, the spend requirement will be exceeded up to 31st March 2030. This position will continue to be monitored.' This suggests execution risk if the housing capital program slips.
findings.matters: Failure to deploy RTB receipts on schedule results in repayment to government with interest, reducing available capital funding and adding unbudgeted cost. Capital program slippage is a material execution risk.
findings.figures: Spend requirement deadline: 31 March 2030; 5-year recycle window from receipt
findings.quote: If the retained receipts are not spent within 5 years, they must be returned to Government with interest. If future actual expenditure matches the budgeted expenditure in the capital programme, the spend requirement will be exceeded up to 31st March 2030. This position will continue to be monitored.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Capital Strategy
findings.headline: The council faces significant revenue budget shortfalls in the medium term and is dependent on invest-to-save schemes to close the gap
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it 'still faces significant shortfalls in its revenue budget in the medium term' and is investing in technology and service transformation schemes to generate ongoing savings. This indicates the council is not in structural balance and requires continuous cost-reduction initiatives.
findings.matters: Revenue shortfalls signal that baseline operating costs exceed funding. If invest-to-save schemes underdeliver or if external income (commercial properties, grants) is disrupted, the council could face a cash shortage or require emergency reserves drawdown.
findings.figures: None specified; invest-to-save dependency is stated without quantified shortfall figures
findings.quote: The Council still faces significant shortfalls in its revenue budget in the medium term. Therefore, it will continue to invest in technologies and programmes which deliver ongoing savings to the Councils finances.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Capital receipts are being gradually eroded, reducing funding flexibility for capital programs
findings.detail: With limited property available for sale and ongoing revenue budget pressures, capital receipts are declining. This erodes the council's ability to fund capital schemes without borrowing or relying on time-limited grants.
findings.matters: Capital receipts fund capital investment without creating revenue charges (no MRP or interest). As receipts shrink, the council must either increase prudential borrowing (with mandatory revenue cost recovery) or depend more heavily on grants that may not be available or sustainable.
findings.figures: Not quantified; described as 'gradually being eroded' with 'limited property available for sale'
findings.quote: However with limited property available for sale, capital receipts are gradually being eroded. And with continuing budgetary pressures being placed on the Council's General Fund the ability to use Direct Revenue Financing (use of reserves) is reducing

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Loan-to-value ratio of 122.65% means prudential borrowing on the commercial property portfolio exceeds the assets' book value
findings.detail: The council financed property acquisitions using prudential borrowing that included acquisition costs (stamp duty, agent fees, legal costs). These financing costs were capitalised but do not increase asset valuation, creating negative equity. While the LTV is forecast to improve to 113.41% by 2028/29 as MRP is charged, the portfolio remains underwater by book value.
findings.matters: If commercial property values fall due to sector weakness, recession, or tenant-quality deterioration, the loan-to-value ratio worsens further, potentially creating a position where debt exceeds realizable disposal value and constrains refinancing options.
findings.quote: In the early years, the loan value is expected to exceed the asset value. The main reason for this is due to acquisition costs e.g. stamp duty, agent fees etc. being included in the cost of the Commercial Property Investments that have been funded by borrowing, these costs are not included in the property valuation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Commercial property investment income—nearly a quarter of service expenditure—is now capped at current 15 properties with no new acquisitions planned
findings.detail: The council holds 15 investment properties (£44.3m value) generating £4.475m gross income in 2025/26, which funds 24.56% of net service expenditure. Following PWLB guidance and CIPFA Prudential Code changes, the council has permanently ceased new acquisitions, meaning this income cannot grow despite continuing service cost inflation.
findings.matters: Revenue funding is now fixed while operational costs continue to rise. Any tenant default or lease non-renewal creates an immediate funding gap with no ability to replace lost income through new investments.
findings.figures: £4.475m gross investment income 2025/26; 24.56% of net service expenditure (forecast); 15 properties; £44.313m portfolio value as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: This highlights the reliance on Commercial Property Investment income in delivering Council services. The strategy for risk mitigation to manage and maintain the income stream is set out in Section 7 of the Commercial Property Investment Strategy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Council holds £15m in LOBO loans with refinancing risk, with two options falling in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The Council holds £15m of LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans where the lender can propose interest rate increases at set dates. Two refinancing options are scheduled for 2025/26. The Council's policy is to repay these at no cost if the opportunity arises, as it is unlikely to take on new LOBO debt in future. The refusal to accept rate increases and preference to repay indicates concern about embedded refinancing risk in this portfolio.
findings.matters: LOBO loans create interest rate refinancing risk: if the lender proposes a higher rate and the Council cannot repay, financing costs could spike unexpectedly. The 2025/26 options represent a material refinancing trigger at a time when the Council is otherwise under financial pressure.
findings.figures: £15m LOBO loans outstanding; two options in 2025/26; current external debt total £82.346m
findings.quote: The Council will take the option to repay LOBO loans at no cost if it has the opportunity to do so. It is unlikely that the Council will take out any new LOBO loans in the future.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: General Fund financing costs rising from 11.60% to 12.93% of net revenue stream over three years.
findings.detail: The affordability indicator showing financing costs (borrowing interest and MRP) as a proportion of the General Fund's core income is forecast to rise from 11.60% in 2025/26 to 12.72% in 2026/27 and 12.93% in 2027/28. This reflects both the increased capital programme and the rising MRP charges needed to repay borrowing. The rising ratio indicates the Council has less financial headroom for service spending.
findings.matters: An increasing ratio signals tightening finances and reduced flexibility to absorb unforeseen pressures. For a lender, it indicates less cushion; for the finance director, it means constrained resources for services. The jump occurs while capital needs are spiking, creating a squeeze.
findings.quote: The Ratio for the General Fund increases from 2026/27 as a result of reduced Government funding and increased MRP charges due to Capital Programme Developments.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Capital expenditure nearly doubles in 2026/27 to £102.7m, requiring £30.6m in new borrowing and £39.9m in reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: Capital expenditure is forecast to jump from £59.9m in 2025/26 to £102.7m in 2026/27, driven by both General Fund (£58.4m) and HRA (£44.3m) programmes. With capital grants declining to £30.8m, the Council plans to fund the gap through £39.9m in direct revenue financing (reserve drawdown) and £30.6m in new external borrowing. Usable reserves are forecast to fall from £123.2m to £112.3m over the three-year period.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to understand the Council's debt trajectory and reserve depletion risk. The reserve-funded portion is unsustainable long-term, while the £30.6m new borrowing (214% increase from prior year) signals tightening financial capacity, especially as financing costs are rising as a proportion of revenue income.
findings.figures: £102.704m capital expenditure 2026/27 (vs £59.870m 2025/26); £30.595m borrowing requirement 2026/27 (vs £9.752m 2025/26); £39.986m direct revenue financing; usable reserves declining to £112.3m
findings.quote: The trajectory of the CFR suggests that the Council may require external borrowing in future years to support its capital plans. However, a recent independent review undertaken by MUFG has revised the CFR estimate downwards to £172m for 24/25, compared with earlier higher projections.

findings.paper_title: Annual Budget and Council Tax 2026/27 and Medium-term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Council is not undertaking the corporate vacancy factor reduction (4% saving) it had previously applied to staff budgets
findings.detail: The council identifies in its savings programmes 'Corporate Vacancy Rates (Previously a 4% vacancy rate reduction was applied across all staff salary budgets. This has now been removed.)'. This removal represents a loss of budgeted savings and suggests either vacancy rates have deteriorated or the council can no longer assume staff turnover will deliver cost savings.
findings.matters: The removal of a 4% vacancy assumption across the salary budget is a sign that staffing levels are normalising or the council cannot rely on turnover savings. This reduces the flexibility in the budget and suggests payroll costs are becoming less controllable.
findings.figures: 4% vacancy rate reduction previously applied; now removed
findings.quote: Corporate Vacancy Rates (Previously a 4% vacancy rate reduction was applied across all staff salary budgets. This has now been removed.)

findings.paper_title: Annual Budget and Council Tax 2026/27 and Medium-term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Capital programme relies heavily on prudential borrowing: £30.595m in General Fund borrowing for 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: The council's £85.572m capital programme for 2026/27 is heavily dependent on prudential borrowing. General Fund prudential borrowing of £30.595m is planned for 2026/27, with a further £7.784m for 2027/28. The Section 151 Officer states the capital programme 'still relies heavily on the Council being prepared to increase its borrowing in future years' and notes 'The impact of the required increase in borrowing is built into the MTFS and will be kept under regular review with the aim of reducing the borrowing need if possible.'
findings.matters: High borrowing levels increase future revenue costs (borrowing and capital financing costs are £2.744m in 2026/27). If interest rates remain elevated or the council's credit rating weakens, borrowing costs could become a material budget pressure.
findings.figures: Prudential borrowing General Fund: £30.595m (2026/27), £7.784m (2027/28); borrowing and capital financing costs budget at £2.744m annually
findings.quote: Prudential Borrowing - General Fund 9,752 30,595 7,784 0 0 48,131

findings.paper_title: Annual Budget and Council Tax 2026/27 and Medium-term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates unquantified cost risk; council sets aside £500k reserve plus £250k in-year spending
findings.detail: The council is undergoing Local Government Reorganisation but the scope and cost remain uncertain. The council has established a £500k reserve in 2025/26 and added £250k to the 2026/27 revenue budget for transition costs. Section 151 Officer notes LGR is 'a risk with expected controls being introduced following the Government consultation' and describes it as an area of 'uncertainty'.
findings.matters: Reorganisation costs are uncontrolled and may exceed the £500k provision. As an event imposed by government with no cost certainty, it poses a material risk to financial stability in a year when the council already faces funding gaps.
findings.figures: £500k LGR reserve; £250k in-year budget allocation for 2026/27
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation is a risk with expected controls being introduced following the Government consultation, these rules will require delivery with corporate discipline.

findings.paper_title: Annual Budget and Council Tax 2026/27 and Medium-term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: The HRA faces medium-term sustainability risk and may need to scale back capital investment in existing properties
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account is balanced in the short term but faces medium-term pressure. The budget notes: 'Whilst there is not an immediate risk to the HRA within the short term the Council must be mindful savings are required within the service itself and from those services and funds that receive contributions from the HRA as well as a potential need to scale back capital investment within existing properties.'
findings.matters: The HRA finances the council's housing stock maintenance and new affordable housing. Scaling back capital investment signals that the council may be unable to sustain its housing maintenance programme or new build ambitions.
findings.figures: HRA capital expenditure: £24.972m in 2026/27; transfer to Major Repairs Reserve increased from £8.646m to £11.143m
findings.quote: Whilst there is not an immediate risk to the HRA within the short term the Council must be mindful savings are required within the service itself and from those services and funds that receive contributions from the HRA as well as a potential need to scale back capital investment within existing properties.

findings.paper_title: Annual Budget and Council Tax 2026/27 and Medium-term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget balanced only by withdrawing £1.985m from earmarked reserves
findings.detail: The proposed 2026/27 budget achieves balance by drawing £1.985m from earmarked reserves: £1.335m from the Revenue Grant Reserve and £650m from the Insurance Reserve. This depletes key reserves in a year when the council faces uncertainty from Local Government Reorganisation. The Section 151 Officer acknowledges that earmarked reserves have been 'repurposed' and notes that this review must 'continue into the new financial year'.
findings.matters: Once-only use of reserves masks an underlying structural deficit and leaves the council with fewer resources to absorb shocks. The depletion of the Insurance Reserve for routine costs reduces protection against unexpected claims.
findings.figures: £1.985m total: £1.335m from Revenue Grant Reserve, £650k from Insurance Reserve
findings.quote: Use of Earmarked Reserves (Revenue Grant Reserve and Insurance Reserve) -1,985

findings.paper_title: Annual Budget and Council Tax 2026/27 and Medium-term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Centre funding falls by £1.025m in 2026/27 with larger gaps emerging in 2027/28 and beyond
findings.detail: The council faces a reduction in central government funding of £1.025m for 2026/27, announced on 10 February 2026. This is followed by further reductions of £452k in 2027/28 and £27k in 2028/29. The MTFS shows estimated funding gaps of £1.875m in 2027/28 and £2.272m in 2028/29 before the use of reserves, leaving a cumulative gap of £1.147m by 2028/29 even after deploying earmarked reserves.
findings.matters: A sustained reduction in government funding forces difficult choices about service sustainability and requires the council to identify £1.875m of new savings in 2027/28 or accept further reserve depletion
findings.figures: £1.025m reduction 2026/27; £452k reduction 2027/28; £27k reduction 2028/29; estimated gap of £1.875m in 2027/28 and £2.272m in 2028/29
findings.quote: Council still sees a reduction in funding of £1.025m for the financial year 2026/27. However, for the budget years of 2027/28 and 2028/29 there is a further funding reduction of £452k and £27k respectively.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Forecast 2026/27 – 2029/30
findings.headline: North Kirkby Gateway scheme carries compliance and viability risks; £2.53m market value transfer flagged for potential undervaluation challenge and Subsidy Control Act violation
findings.detail: One recommendation is to appropriate 20 apartments from the North Kirkby Gateway development into the HRA at market value (£2,533,333). The report flags that this option carries financial exposure if the scheme does not meet the council's financial viability model. Legislative compliance risks include audit scrutiny if the market value transfer is challenged as undervalued, potentially triggering Subsidy Control Act violations with clawback or fines. Operational risks include £50,000 annual staffing cost for maintenance and potential delays if HRA borrowing headroom is constrained (estimated HRA debt £150 million).
findings.matters: This is a specific transaction with flagged compliance risks. A lender needs to understand whether the scheme meets the council's investment appraisal standard and whether the valuation could be challenged post-appropriation, creating contingent liability.
findings.figures: £2,533,333 market value; £50,000 estimated annual maintenance staff cost; £150 million estimated HRA debt (against an understood debt cap)
findings.quote: While beneficial, this option carries risks, including financial exposure to the HRA with the scheme not meeting the financial viability model set by the council. Legislative compliance risks arise if the market value transfer is challenged as undervalued, leading to audit scrutiny or Subsidy Control Act violations, which could result in clawback or fines.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Forecast 2026/27 – 2029/30
findings.headline: Mandatory social housing regulator inspection by March 2028; compliance with Awaab's Law and new professional qualification requirements adding staffing costs
findings.detail: The council has not yet been inspected by the Regulator of Social Housing, but inspections are mandatory by March 2028 and can occur at short notice. The Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023 brought in new Consumer Standards. Awaab's Law compliance launched October 2025 with further hazards to be phased in 2026–2027. The council has already added staffing resources and is considering further additions. Regulatory fees are circa £52,000 annually; Housing Ombudsman membership fee circa £55,000 annually.
findings.matters: This is a near-term regulatory event (mandatory by 2028) with material cost implications. Compliance failure could result in enforcement action, reputation damage, or enforcement expenditure. The council is already escalating staffing; failure to meet standards could trigger costly remediation.
findings.figures: Regulator of Social Housing annual fee circa £52,000; Housing Ombudsman annual membership fee circa £55,000; specialist damp, mould and disrepair team created; further staffing resources being considered
findings.quote: Actions continue to be implemented to ensure that the council's compliance with the Regulator of Social Housing's statutory Consumer Standards is as robust as possible. Six monthly updates are provided to Cabinet; the latest update having been presented in January 2026. To date additional resources have been added to the establishment to assist with maintaining regulatory compliance and further additional staffing resources are currently being considered to assist with increasing complexities of regulation and the tenant demographic, including the handling of increasing complaint volumes.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Forecast 2026/27 – 2029/30
findings.headline: Carbon net zero retrofitting unaffordable within self-financing model; £20m estimated cost cannot be met without government funding
findings.detail: The council estimates an average cost of £20,000 per property to retrofit the housing stock to carbon net-zero standards by 2050. The document models this scenario (Graph 2) against the 30-year business plan and concludes that without additional government funding, the HRA balance would become insolvent within the planning horizon. Current ambition is to upgrade stock to EPC Band C by 2030, broadly costing £10m.
findings.matters: This represents a material, legislated long-term liability (UK legally obliged to reach net-zero by 2050) that the current revenue and reserve model cannot absorb. Lenders need to know whether government will fund this gap or force councils to borrow heavily.
findings.figures: £20,000 per property average retrofit cost (indicative, no inflationary adjustment); £10m estimated cost to upgrade to EPC Band C by 2030; Graph 2 shows projected balance would trend negative if £20k cost is incurred
findings.quote: This shows that without Government funding the carbon net zero target cannot be met within the current self-financing model of the HRA.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Forecast 2026/27 – 2029/30
findings.headline: 2026 stock condition survey expected to drive upward revision of capital expenditure and inflationary cost pressures
findings.detail: The council's asset maintenance forecast relies on a stock condition survey last done in 2018. A new full survey is expected in 2026 and will revalue capital expenditure requirements over the next 30 years. The report explicitly notes this will have a 'negative effect on the plan', accounting for changed stock levels, component lifespans, new legislative requirements, and inflationary pressures.
findings.matters: This is a known but unquantified downside to the financial plan. The current 5-year forecast assumes £121.56m capital spend; the 2026 survey revaluation could require material upward revision, reducing reserve depletion buffers further.
findings.figures: Current HRA capital programme 2025–2030: £121.56m; stock condition survey last undertaken in 2018
findings.quote: the next full survey will take place in 2026 and will lead to a revaluation of capital expenditure considering new legislative requirements and inflationary cost pressures (this will have a negative effect on the plan).

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Forecast 2026/27 – 2029/30
findings.headline: Universal Credit creating structural arrears risk through payment delays and deductions affecting vulnerable tenants
findings.detail: As of 15 December 2025, 3,702 UC cases and 1,362 Housing Benefit cases are outstanding. UC is paid monthly in arrears rather than weekly, creating a 'saw-tooth' debt pattern. Arrears spike significantly in the first 8–12 weeks after a UC claim starts. Third-party deductions for other debts can be up to 40%, leaving vulnerable tenants unable to pay rent after deductions, and some tenants now worse off on UC than under previous benefits.
findings.matters: This is an active mechanism eroding rental income on a large scale (3,702 cases) affecting the HRA's financial sustainability. The bad debt provision in the forecast assumes 1% of gross rental income, but the document signals this may be inadequate if UC-driven arrears accelerate.
findings.figures: 3,702 UC cases as of 15 December 2025; 1,362 HB cases; bad debt provision 1% of gross rental income (£313k–£372k per year in the forecast)
findings.quote: Universal Credit is significantly impacting on council housing rent arrears with the Department of Work and Pensions paying monthly benefits (personal and housing costs) to tenants in arrears, creating a pattern where short term arrears build up before the monthly payment, often leading to spikes in debt, especially in the first few months of a claim, due to the five-week wait, pushing vulnerable tenants into hardship and increasing arrears.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Forecast 2026/27 – 2029/30
findings.headline: HRA reserves depleting sharply over five years from £51.5m to £4.6m, driven by major capital programme
findings.detail: The council's HRA balance will fall from £51.5m at 31 March 2025 to £4.6m by 31 March 2030. This decline is driven primarily by funding the capital programme from reserves rather than borrowing. The minimum balance the council holds is £2.5m, leaving limited buffer for unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls by 2030.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's capacity to absorb financial shocks is shrinking rapidly. A reserve of £4.6m on an annual HRA turnover of £32m is thin; regulatory inspections starting 2026 could demand remedial spending.
findings.figures: £51.5m opening balance, £4.6m closing balance by 2030/31; minimum balance £2.5m; HRA annual turnover circa £32m (2025/26)
